paper.title: WoCoCo: Learning Whole-Body Humanoid Control with Sequential Contacts

decision_relevance.why_admitted: WoCoCo is a direct, source-located example of composing a long-horizon task into an ordered contact-stage oracle and coupling that oracle state to dense contact, stage-progress, and exploration rewards. Its ablations expose reward-stalling and under-exploration failure modes that Sam's harness should test while holding the trainer fixed.
not_evidence_for: Automatic search, ranking, or composition of reference datasets
A learned, branching, or predicate-synthesized oracle
Reference-motion tracking or dynamics feasibility of a composed motion
An oracle-only or reward-only causal effect under a frozen trainer, observation space, curriculum, and controller
A complete public reproduction of all four humanoid tasks

mechanisms.name: Contact-stage specification
mechanisms.description: A task is manually decomposed into an ordered sequence of stages. Each stage contains a contact goal for selected end effectors and an additional task goal; stage fulfillment requires both goals simultaneously.

mechanisms.name: Feedback-gated linear stage automaton
mechanisms.description: Contact or human feedback marks the current stage fulfilled; after a predefined dwell period, an integer stage index advances monotonically to the next predefined stage.

mechanisms.name: Goal-conditioned whole-body policy
mechanisms.description: The end-to-end policy receives proprioception and a task-specific representation of the active or near-future contact/task goals, then emits joint position targets for a low-level PD controller.

mechanisms.name: Oracle-coupled reward stack
mechanisms.description: The reward sums task-agnostic contact/stage/curiosity terms, task-agnostic sim-to-real regularizers, and one or two task-specific terms; several components read the automaton's stage state or goal predicates.

mechanisms.name: Dense correct/wrong-contact reward
mechanisms.description: Every correct end-effector contact contributes positively, wrong contacts are penalized after the first stage, and simultaneous contact/task-goal fulfillment receives a quadratic-in-end-effectors bonus.

mechanisms.name: Task-gated stage-count reward
mechanisms.description: The reward pays the number of completed stages only while the task goal is fulfilled, intended to counter policies that stay in an easy stage to avoid later risk.

mechanisms.name: Random-hash count curiosity
mechanisms.description: A frozen random neural network maps normalized base/end-effector state to a binary hash bucket; intrinsic reward decays with the bucket visit count and is symmetry averaged.

mechanisms.name: Three-phase sim-to-real curriculum
mechanisms.description: Training proceeds without domain randomization, then with domain randomization, then with progressively stronger regularization; curiosity is active only in phase one.

mechanisms.name: Paper training and control stack
mechanisms.description: PPO with symmetry augmentation trains end-to-end MLP actor/critic networks in Isaac Gym; actions are joint position targets tracked by a higher-rate PD loop.

mechanisms.name: Clap-and-dance public demonstration
mechanisms.description: The pinned repository exposes one H1 jump-jack/clap-and-dance reward and MDP example, not the full parkour, box, cliffside, and dinosaur experiment suite.

failure_modes.name: Intentional stage stalling
failure_modes.description: Without the stage-count term, the parkour policy intentionally avoids satisfying the active contact goal so it need not enter harder later stages.

failure_modes.name: Sparse-contact under-exploration
failure_modes.description: The 0-1 contact baseline and the no-curiosity ablation remain in posture-tracking behavior instead of jumping over the stones.

failure_modes.name: RND risky-behavior attractor
failure_modes.description: The RND baseline leans backward in a risky posture, which the authors interpret as over-exploring rare but behaviorally unhelpful states.

failure_modes.name: Unknown-length stage-count exploitation
failure_modes.description: The authors warn that if sequence length is not known a priori, the stage-count reward may require heuristic clamping to prevent exploitation.

failure_modes.name: No controller failure predictor
failure_modes.description: Unlike a model-based solver, the learned controller does not provide a feasibility/failure certificate.

failure_modes.name: External stage-transition feedback
failure_modes.description: Stage switching requires explicit contact feedback from sensors or human observers; transition predicates are not inferred by the policy.

failure_modes.name: Heuristic predefined oracle
failure_modes.description: The contact sequence and stage partition are supplied by humans; the work does not learn or optimize the oracle itself.

failure_modes.name: Single-task reward ablations
failure_modes.description: Reward ablations and five-seed stability plots are run on parkour; the paper does not repeat them across the other humanoid tasks.

failure_modes.name: Goal-lookahead description inconsistency
failure_modes.description: Appendix H says non-parkour tasks receive only the current stage, but the cliffside subsection says its policy receives current and next-stage goal regions.

failure_modes.name: Partial public implementation
failure_modes.description: The official repository explicitly provides a clap-and-dance example, so it cannot by itself reproduce the paper's full task suite or every reported reward configuration.

failure_modes.name: Paper/code curiosity mismatch
failure_modes.description: The paper reports preprocessing method (2) and 1/sqrt(visits); the public demo applies stage-index rescaling and increments the count before evaluating 1/sqrt(1+count).

failure_modes.name: Fixed-trainer confound
failure_modes.description: The paper's method jointly changes policy goal observations, reward, curiosity, domain randomization, regularization schedule, and low-level deployment details; it is not evidence that changing only Sam's oracle or task reward improves a frozen trainer.

evaluation.name: Five-task, two-embodiment demonstration suite
evaluation.description: The paper demonstrates parkour, box loco-manipulation, clap-and-tap dancing, and cliffside climbing on humanoids, plus 22-DoF dinosaur ball loco-manipulation; the four humanoid policies are shown in real-world demonstrations.

evaluation.name: Parkour reward-component ablation
evaluation.description: The reported 0-1-contact, no-stage-count, no-curiosity, and RND-curiosity variants exhibit distinct failure behaviors; these results are qualitative/curve-based and restricted to parkour.

evaluation.name: Five-seed parkour learning curves
evaluation.description: Curiosity and normalized task-progress curves are plotted for five random seeds, but no tabulated confidence interval or hypothesis test is reported.

evaluation.name: Sim-to-real curriculum ablation
evaluation.description: Moving domain randomization into phase one reduces parkour average progress below 0.6 versus above 0.75; omitting phase three yields jerky real-world cliffside behavior and step-out failures.

evaluation.name: Real-world evidence boundary
evaluation.description: Results are demonstrations without a tabulated hardware success rate; real parkour is limited to double-foot sequences with one or two continuous jumps because of facility constraints.

evaluation.name: Pinned public-code audit
evaluation.description: At commit c44d312, the release contains one constrained 10-stage clap-and-dance environment and exposes paper-like contact/progress/curiosity terms, but it is a partial implementation and contains curiosity details that differ from the paper text.

evidence.claim: The reviewed paper is arXiv:2406.06005v2, revised 7 November 2024, by Chong Zhang, Wenli Xiao, Tairan He, and Guanya Shi.
A task is manually decomposed into ordered contact stages; each requires simultaneous contact- and task-goal fulfillment, and sensors or human observers trigger advancement after a predefined dwell.

evidence.locator: Section 2, Equation 1 and final two paragraphs
evidence.claim: The policy is goal-conditioned; reward separates WoCoCo/regularization/task terms; PPO with symmetry augmentation trains an end-to-end MLP in Isaac Gym; actions are joint targets tracked by PD control.
WoCoCo sums dense contact, stage-count, and curiosity terms; the paper gives exact dense-contact and task-gated stage-count formulas and their anti-local-optimum rationale.
A frozen random neural network creates a sign-bit hash bucket, and the paper's intrinsic reward is the inverse square root of that bucket's visit count.

The three-phase curriculum delays domain randomization, then increases regularization weights by 20 percent every 2000 iterations until doubled; curiosity is active only in phase one and three control steps are stacked.
The paper demonstrates four humanoid tasks in simulation and hardware and a 22-DoF dinosaur task; real parkour is limited to one or two double-foot jumps because of facility constraints.
Parkour ablations report failure with 0-1 contacts, intentional stalling without stage reward, under-exploration without curiosity, and risky leaning with RND; stability curves use five seeds.

Reported limitations include no failure predictor, potential stage-count exploitation for unknown sequence length, heuristic contact sequences, motion-capture dependence, and explicit stage-transition feedback.
The table reports per-task contact, stage, and curiosity weights for parkour, box loco-manipulation, dancing, and cliffside climbing.
The paper specifies the shared regularization terms, formulas, and weights, including task-conditional feet-air-time and no-fly shaping.
The appendix gives exact task-specific reward formulas and constants for the four humanoid tasks.

Policies combine proprioception with task-specific goal representations and use 512-256-128 MLPs; the general lookahead statement and cliffside subsection disagree about whether cliffside receives next-stage goals.
Curiosity uses base and end-effector state, a one-hidden-layer 32-unit hash network with 16 outputs, and the reported experiments use sine/cosine preprocessing without stage rescaling.
The appendix reports friction, mass, center-of-mass, gain, control-delay, torque-noise, push, and terrain randomization ranges.
Starting domain randomization in phase one yields parkour progress below 0.6 versus above 0.75; removing phase three produces jerky cliffside behavior and real-world step-out failures.
Deployment uses a 50 Hz policy, 200 Hz PD loop, and a 4 Hz Butterworth filter on PD targets; robot geometry and mass were corrected from the official URDF.

evidence.claim: The public demo stores a four-end-effector contact sequence and current stage index, advances after fulfillment plus a dwell timer, and exposes the active phase in the policy observation.
The public demo implements whole-body fulfillment, dense correct/wrong-contact scoring, stage-progress reward, and base/end-effector curiosity observations.
The demo's hash curiosity symmetry-averages observations, multiplies normalized features by stage index plus one, increments the bucket count, then computes 1/sqrt(1+count).
The demo config pins contact/progress/curiosity scales 10/5/5000, 29 curiosity inputs, a 32-unit hidden layer, 16 hash bits, a 10-stage sequence, and 0.4-0.8 second contact periods.
